mainEntity.name: How much does a Mercedes-Benz CLC 200 CDI or 220 CDI engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A replacement OM646 engine for a CLC 200 CDI or 220 CDI typically costs between £800 and £3,200 depending on condition and engine code. Used units start from £800-£1,600, reconditioned from £1,400-£2,800, and fully rebuilt from £1,800-£3,200. Labour for supply & fit adds £500-£900. A replacement OM646.963 engine costs on average £1,246 in good condition, with reconditioned units costing up to £1,495.

mainEntity.name: What is swirl flap failure and does it affect the CLC 200 CDI / 220 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Swirl flap failure is the #1 diesel killer in OM646 engines. Plastic swirl flaps in the inlet manifold can break and be ingested into cylinders, causing catastrophic piston, valve, and cylinder head damage. Symptoms include loss of power, limp mode, a hissing intake sound, and fault codes P2004 or P2006. The permanent fix is swirl flap removal and blanking (£400-£800) - not replacement with another plastic manifold.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between the CLC 200 CDI and CLC 220 CDI engines?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both use the OM646 2.1-litre four-cylinder turbodiesel, but with different power outputs. The CLC 200 CDI uses the OM646.981 producing 122 hp (90 kW) and 270 Nm torque. The CLC 220 CDI uses the OM646.980 producing 150 hp (110 kW) and 330 Nm torque. Both share the same basic architecture, common-rail injection, and variable geometry turbocharger.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in a Mercedes-Benz CLC 200 CDI or 220 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the car's condition and mileage. A CLC 200 CDI or 220 CDI is typically worth £2,000-£5,000 - a rebuilt OM646 engine (£1,800-£3,200) can be a worthwhile investment if the car is in good condition. For lower-value examples, a targeted repair (swirl flap delete, injector seals) may be more economical than a full replacement.

mainEntity.name: What causes the Mercedes-Benz CLC 200 CDI / 220 CDI to lose power?

acceptedAnswer.text: Power loss in the CLC 200 CDI and 220 CDI is most commonly caused by EGR valve clogging from carbon deposits, turbocharger issues (sticking variable vanes), or swirl flap failure. Injector seal leakage can also cause compression loss and reduced performance. A diagnostic check with Mercedes STAR or compatible equipment is essential to identify the exact cause.

mainEntity.name: Is the OM646 engine reliable in the CLC 200 CDI and 220 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: The OM646 is generally robust and capable of 200,000-400,000 miles with proper maintenance. However, it has well-documented weak points: swirl flap collapse (the #1 failure driver), injector seal leakage, and EGR valve clogging. Addressing swirl flaps preventatively with a delete kit is the single most important thing you can do to ensure long-term reliability.

historyTimeline.h2: Mercedes-Benz CLC 200 CDI / 220 CDI - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The CLC 200 CDI and CLC 220 CDI represented the diesel backbone of the Mercedes-Benz CLC range throughout its 2008-2011 production run. Both variants used the same OM646 2.1-litre four-cylinder turbodiesel engine, with the CLC 200 CDI receiving a lower-output tune and the CLC 220 CDI offering additional power. The CL203 platform - a heavily updated version of the C-Class Sports Coupe - housed these engines with over 1,100 new components introduced for the CLC rebranding.

problems.h4: OM646 Swirl Flap Collapse - The #1 Diesel Killer in the CLC 200 / 220 CDI
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes-Benz CLC 200 CDI and 220 CDI (OM646.981 and OM646.980, 2008-2011)
problems.rootCause: The OM646's inlet manifold contains plastic swirl flaps that regulate airflow for emissions. Over time, EGR carbon buildup causes flaps to seize, and the plastic pivot points can snap. A broken flap can be ingested directly into a cylinder, causing catastrophic piston, valve, and cylinder head damage.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Removal of all flaps, blanking of pivot holes in the manifold, ECU remap to delete fault codes
repairOptions.longevity: Permanent solution. Eliminates future flap failure risk entirely

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit of rebuilt OM646 with swirl flap delete or upgraded manifold
repairOptions.longevity: Required if flap ingestion has destroyed the cylinder head or pistons

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical CLC 200 CDI or 220 CDI is worth £2,000-£5,000 depending on condition and mileage. For vehicles under £3,500, a swirl flap removal and blanking (£400-£800) is the clear choice - it permanently eliminates the failure risk. If flap ingestion has already occurred, a rebuilt OM646 engine (£1,800-£3,200) is usually the most cost-effective solution.
problems.recommendation: The moment a swirl flap fault code appears (often accompanied by limp mode or a hissing intake sound), arrange flap removal immediately. Dealer pricing for a new manifold is prohibitive at £1,200+. Specialist flap removal and blanking costs a fraction of that and permanently solves the issue. For pre-2010 CLC models, this is the sensible long-term fix.
problems.cta: -> Get quotes for OM646 swirl flap repair on your CLC 200 CDI / 220 CDI

problems.h4: OM646 Injector Seal Leakage - Diesel Combustion Knock and Poor Starting
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes-Benz CLC 200 CDI and 220 CDI (OM646.981 and OM646.980, 2008-2011)
problems.rootCause: The copper washer seal between the injector and cylinder head degrades over time, allowing combustion gases to escape past the seal. This creates a characteristic ticking or chuffing noise and can lead to injector seizure if ignored.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Remove one injector, clean seat, replace copper washer and clamp bolt
repairOptions.longevity: Viable if caught early; prevents injector seizure

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: All four injector seals replaced, carbon removal from bores, leak-off testing
repairOptions.longevity: For moderate carbon buildup; specialist approach significantly cheaper

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete engine with new injectors and seals
repairOptions.longevity: Required if injector seizure has caused cylinder head damage

problems.recommendation: If you hear a ticking or chuffing noise from the engine bay that changes with engine speed, have the injector seals inspected. Replacing all four seals at a specialist costs £450-£750 and is far cheaper than the £1,800+ bill for injector replacement if they seize.
problems.cta: -> Get quotes for OM646 injector seal replacement for your CLC 200 CDI / 220 CDI

problems.h4: OM646 EGR Valve & Turbocharger Issues - Reduced Power and Hesitation
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes-Benz CLC 200 CDI and 220 CDI (OM646.981 and OM646.980, 2008-2011)
problems.rootCause: The EGR valve can become clogged with carbon deposits, particularly on vehicles used for short journeys. The variable geometry turbocharger can suffer from sticking vanes due to carbon buildup, causing loss of boost and reduced power.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Remove and clean EGR valve; or replace if necessary
repairOptions.longevity: Viable; carbon buildup is the main cause

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace or rebuild turbocharger, oil feed lines
repairOptions.longevity: Required if turbo has failed or vanes are seized

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete engine with new turbo and EGR components
repairOptions.longevity: Only if turbo failure has caused engine damage

problems.recommendation: If your CLC 200 CDI or 220 CDI experiences loss of power, have the turbocharger and EGR system inspected. A £300-£600 EGR clean or £800-£1,500 turbo repair is significantly cheaper than a full engine replacement. Regular motorway driving helps keep the EGR and turbo vanes clear.
